pos: v. (past of forge; beaten out on an anvil; hence, fabricated)
etymology: French forger, Latin fabricari, to frame or fashion, from faber, a smith. The smith's word, carried over to the fabrication of a falsehood.
biblical_def: A forged thing is a made thing — hammered, shaped, and finished with labour. That is why the psalmist chooses the smith's word for slander: “The proud have forged a lie against me: but I will keep thy precepts with my whole heart” (Psalm 119:69). The lie was not a careless word dropped in passing; it was worked. Someone heated it, beat it into shape, and brought it out finished. Scripture is honest about the industry of the ungodly: the ninth commandment is broken by craftsmen, not only by fools. And the psalmist's answer is not counter-forgery but fidelity — but I will keep thy precepts. He does not meet the hammer with a hammer. He holds the law. The next verse names what makes a man able to forge: “Their heart is as fat as grease; but I delight in thy law” (Psalm 119:70). A conscience greased over feels nothing as the lie is shaped. This is the one place the Authorized Version uses the word, and it is worth the whole of Psalm 119 to see it: the believer under manufactured slander has one refuge, and it is the written word of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FORGED, participle passive Hammered; beaten into shape; made; fabricated; counterfeited.
webster_full: FORGED, participle passive Hammered; beaten into shape by the hammer.
2. Made; framed; contrived; devised.
3. Falsely made; counterfeited; as a forged signature.
FORGE, verb transitive To form by heating and hammering; to beat into any particular shape, as a metal.
2. To make by any means; to counterfeit; as, to forge a tale; to forge a lie.
scriptures: The proud have forged a lie against me: but I will keep thy precepts with my whole heart.
Their heart is as fat as grease; but I delight in thy law.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
corruption_summary: Slander is now called narrative, framing, or messaging, as though manufacture of a falsehood were a neutral craft.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern trade has given the forged lie respectable names. A fabrication worked up to destroy a man is called a narrative; the workshop is called communications; the hammering is called framing. Renaming the forge does not cool it. Scripture names the thing by what it is — a lie, forged, against a neighbour — and sets it under the ninth commandment without softening.

The principle to recover is the psalmist's reply. He does not answer the forge in kind, and he does not collapse. He keeps the precepts with his whole heart, and he delights in the law while the lie is still in circulation. Vindication is God's business; fidelity is ours.

pos: v. (past of engage; pledged; bound by promise; set in earnest)
etymology: French engager, to pledge, from en- and gage, a pledge. In Jeremiah 30:21 it renders the Hebrew 'arab, to pledge or become surety.
biblical_def: The Authorized Version uses engaged once, and it is a messianic astonishment: “And their nobles shall be of themselves, and their governor shall proceed from the midst of them; and I will cause him to draw near, and he shall approach unto me: for who is this that engaged his heart to approach unto me? saith the LORD” (Jeremiah 30:21). The question is not rhetorical flattery. Sinful men do not engage their hearts to approach a holy God; they hide, as Adam hid. So the LORD asks who this is — and the answer stands in the same verse: I will cause him to draw near. The approach is the Lord's doing, and the Governor who comes from the midst of His people is the one Man whose heart was pledged to that approach from eternity. The Hebrew behind it is the word for surety: he put himself in pledge. That is precisely the office of Christ, who became surety of a better testament (Hebrews 7:22). The covenant promise follows immediately: “And ye shall be my people, and I will be your God” (Jeremiah 30:22). The engaged heart of the Mediator is the ground of the restored nation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ENGAGED, participle passive Pledged; promised; enlisted; gained; occupied; earnest.
webster_full: ENGAGED, participle passive Pledged; promised.
2. Enlisted; embarked in an affair.
3. Gained and attached; as the affections.
4. Occupied; employed; busied.
5. Earnest; zealous; as, the parties are warmly engaged.

And ye shall be my people, and I will be your God.
Heb 7:22
By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament.
corruption_summary: Engagement is now a word for attention and activity; Scripture uses it of a heart put in pledge.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern speech has emptied the word. To be engaged now means to be interested, occupied, or present — engagement is measured in clicks and attendance. Jeremiah's word is a legal pledge: a man binds himself as surety, puts his own person in the gap, and cannot withdraw. The flattening of the word has made it harder to read the verse at all.

The principle to recover is that the approach of a sinner to God is never self-initiated. Jeremiah 30:21 asks who could engage his heart to draw near, and answers in the same breath: I will cause him to draw near. The Mediator's pledge, not our interest, is what opens the way.

pos: v. (past of erect; set upright; raised and built)
etymology: Latin erigere, erectus, to set upright, from e- and regere, to direct or make straight. In Genesis 33:20 it renders the Hebrew natsab, to set up or station.
biblical_def: Jacob comes home. He has crossed Jordan, met Esau, bought a parcel of ground at Shechem, and then does the thing that marks every stage of patriarchal obedience: “And he erected there an altar, and called it Elelohe-Israel” (Genesis 33:20). The name means God, the God of Israel — and Israel is the new name Jacob himself had received at Peniel. He is not naming the altar after himself; he is confessing that the God who wrestled him and renamed him is the God he will worship on this ground. An altar erected is a stake driven: this land, this household, this generation belongs to the LORD. Abraham had done the same at Shechem a hundred years before (Genesis 12:7). The verb is deliberate — set upright, stationed, made to stand. Nothing in the patriarchal narratives is built for display; the altars are small, stony, and permanent in testimony rather than in stone. The Authorized Version uses erected here alone, and it belongs to worship, not architecture. Where a man settles, he raises an altar, or he has not truly settled.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ERECTED, participle passive Raised; set upright; built; established.
webster_full: ERECTED, participle passive Raised; set in a straight and perpendicular direction.
2. Built; raised; as a building.
3. Established; as a new company or society.
ERECT, verb transitive To raise and set in a perpendicular direction; to set upright.
2. To raise, as a building; to build; to construct; as, to erect an altar.
scriptures: And he erected there an altar, and called it Elelohe-Israel.

Gen 12:7

corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: The one misuse worth naming is sentimental: the patriarchal altars are sometimes read as personal spiritual markers, moments of private meaning. They are nothing of the kind. An altar is where blood is shed for sin, and Jacob's altar at Shechem confesses the same substitution Abraham confessed on the same ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that worship marks possession. Jacob bought the field and erected the altar in the same chapter; a Christian household that settles anywhere without family worship has pitched a tent and raised nothing.

pos: v. (past of undertake; took upon oneself; engaged to do)
etymology: English under and take — to take a thing upon oneself, to get under its weight. In Esther 9:23 it renders the Hebrew qibbel, to receive or take upon oneself.
biblical_def: “And the Jews undertook to do as they had begun, and as Mordecai had written unto them” (Esther 9:23). The word marks the moment a deliverance becomes a discipline. God had broken Haman's plot; the Jews had been given their lives; and now they take upon themselves a yearly remembrance, not because the law of Moses commanded it but because Mordecai wrote and they received it. The Hebrew is the word for receiving a thing as binding. Esther 9:27 spells out how far they bound themselves: upon them, upon their seed, and upon all such as joined themselves unto them. This is how thanksgiving hardens into habit, and habit into inheritance. Scripture does not treat a self-imposed remembrance as equal to a divine command — Purim is not a Levitical feast, and the dictionary holds the regulative principle for corporate worship. But in the household and the calendar, a people who have been spared may rightly undertake to remember, and to teach their children to remember. What is undertaken lightly is dropped lightly; what is undertaken as the Jews undertook it survives twenty-five centuries.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): UNDERTOOK, preterit tense of undertake. To engage in; to take upon oneself.
webster_full: UNDERTOOK, preterit tense of undertake.
UNDERTAKE, verb transitive To engage in; to enter upon; to take in hand; to set about.
2. To covenant or contract to perform.
3. To attempt; to try.
4. To assume a character.
scriptures: Est 9:23
And the Jews undertook to do as they had begun, and as Mordecai had written unto them;
Est 9:22
That they should make them days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor.
Deu 6:7
And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up.
corruption_summary: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors crowd this verse. The first makes Purim a divine ordinance and so blurs the line Scripture keeps between what God commands in worship and what a people lawfully undertake in memory. The dictionary holds the regulative principle: what Scripture commands in corporate worship is required, and what it has not commanded is not permitted there.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the opposite error's cure: a household may and should bind itself to remember God's mercies. The Jews undertook, and their seed after them, and the memory held. Deliverance that is never undertaken as a discipline is forgotten within a generation.

pos: v. (past of decide; determined; settled by sentence)
etymology: Latin decidere, to cut off, from de- and caedere, to cut. A decision cuts a matter through so that it cannot be reopened.
biblical_def: The prophet comes to Ahab disguised, tells a parable of a servant who let a prisoner escape, and invites the king to pass sentence. Ahab passes it: “And as thy servant was busy here and there, he was gone. And the king of Israel said unto him, So shall thy judgment be; thyself hast decided it” (1 Kings 20:40). The sentence is just, swift, and fatal — and it is his own. Ahab had let Benhadad go, a man God had appointed to destruction, and now out of his own mouth the verdict falls: “therefore thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people” (1 Kings 20:42). Scripture uses this device more than once: Nathan with David, the prophet with Ahab, the Lord with the Pharisees in the parable of the vineyard. A man will see a case clearly when he does not know it is his own. The Latin behind decide is to cut off, and that is the force here. Ahab did not offer an opinion; he cut the matter through. The Authorized Version uses the word once, and it stands as a warning that the judgment we pronounce on others is a judgment we have already accepted for ourselves.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): DECIDED, participle passive Determined; settled; ended; concluded.
webster_full: DECIDED, participle passive Determined; settled; ended; concluded.
2. Free from doubt; as a decided opinion.
DECIDE, verb transitive To end; to determine, as a controversy, by cutting off debate.
2. To determine the event of; as, to decide a battle.
3. To settle; to fix the issue of a question.
scriptures: And the king of Israel said unto him, So shall thy judgment be; thyself hast decided it.
Because thou hast let go out of thy hand a man whom I appointed to utter destruction, therefore thy life shall go for his life, and thy people for his people.
Mat 7:2
For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
corruption_summary: Decision is now spoken of as a process to be kept open; Scripture treats it as a cut that cannot be uncut.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic register prefers decisions that remain reversible — a journey, a season of discernment, a position held lightly. The Latin is against it: to decide is to cut off. Ahab's word was final the moment he spoke it, and the prophet held him to it. Scripture everywhere treats sentence, vow, and verdict as binding on the one who utters them.

The principle to recover is Matthew 7:2. The standard a man applies to another is the standard already applied to him. Ahab judged the careless servant and sentenced Ahab; this is not poetic irony but the ordinary working of divine justice.

pos: v. (past of uphold; held up; sustained)
etymology: English up and hold. In Isaiah 63:5 it renders the Hebrew samak, to lean upon, support, sustain.
biblical_def: Isaiah 63 shows the Conqueror coming from Edom with dyed garments, and then gives the reason He came alone: “And I looked, and there was none to help; and I wondered that there was none to uphold: therefore mine own arm brought salvation unto me; and my fury, it upheld me” (Isaiah 63:5). Two uses of one root stand in a single verse. There was none to uphold Him; His fury upheld Him. The sentence is a statement of the solitude of redemption. “I have trodden the winepress alone; and of the people there was none with me” (Isaiah 63:3). No creature contributed to the work; no ally lent strength; the arm that brought salvation was His own, and the zeal that sustained Him in it was His own righteous anger against sin. This is the Reformed doctrine of accomplished redemption in prophetic dress. Christ did not find help and could not have used it. What upheld Him through the treading was not sympathy but holiness — a settled fury against the iniquity He was crushing. The Authorized Version uses upheld once, and it is here, at the point where salvation is shown to be monergistic from first to last.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): UPHELD, preterit tense and participle passive of uphold. Sustained; supported.
webster_full: UPHELD, preterit tense and participle passive of uphold.
UPHOLD, verb transitive To lift on high; to elevate.
2. To support; to sustain; to keep from falling or slipping.
3. To keep from declension.
4. To continue without failing; to keep in being.
scriptures: Isa 63:5

And he saw that there was no man, and wondered that there was no intercessor: therefore his arm brought salvation unto him; and his righteousness, it sustained him.
corruption_summary: Redemption is widely presented as a cooperation; Isaiah 63:5 says there was none to uphold and the arm was His own.
corruption_paragraphs: Every synergistic scheme — Roman merit, Arminian prevenient cooperation, the modern invitation that makes the decisive act the sinner's — must find a creature somewhere in the winepress. Isaiah 63:5 forecloses it: there was none to uphold. Not insufficient help, not unworthy help: none. The arm that brought salvation was His own.

The principle to recover is that the same verse grounds assurance. If no creature upheld Christ in the accomplishing, no creature's failure can unmake it. Isaiah 59:16 says the identical thing of the intercessor: there was no man, so His own righteousness sustained Him.

pos: v. (past of stiffen; made rigid; hardened)
etymology: English stiff, Saxon stif, rigid, unbending. In 2 Chronicles 36:13 it renders the Hebrew qashah, to be hard, used with 'oreph, the neck.
biblical_def: The last king of Judah is summed up in one sentence: “And he also rebelled against king Nebuchadnezzar, who had made him swear by God: but he stiffened his neck, and hardened his heart from turning unto the LORD God of Israel” (2 Chronicles 36:13). Zedekiah broke an oath sworn by God and would not be turned. The Chronicler's verdict is the dictionary's verdict. Note the order: the neck first, then the heart. The stiff neck is the outward refusal to bow the head; the hard heart is the inward refusal to feel. Scripture uses the image from Exodus onward of a people who will not take the yoke — an ox that will not bend its neck to the collar cannot be driven. And note who does the stiffening: he stiffened his neck. Judicial hardening by God is real (Exodus 9:12; Romans 9:18), but it never erases the sinner's own act. The chapter ends with the temple burned and the people carried to Babylon, and the Chronicler gives the reason without ambiguity: “till there was no remedy” (2 Chronicles 36:16). A neck stiffened long enough becomes a nation's grave.

webster_full: STIFFENED, participle passive Made stiff.

Pro 29:1

corruption_summary: Hardening is now treated as damage done to a man; Scripture treats it here as a man's own act, and judicially righteous.
corruption_paragraphs: The therapeutic reading makes a hard heart a wound — something that happened to Zedekiah rather than something Zedekiah did. The Chronicler will not have it. He stiffened his neck; he hardened his heart; he broke an oath sworn by God. Sin is the category, not injury, and the remedy is repentance, not recovery.

The principle to recover is Proverbs 29:1. Reproof refused does not leave a man where he was; it leaves him harder. There is a point at which the Chronicler records no remedy — not because God's mercy ran out, but because the neck would not bend. That is a warning to be preached, not softened.

pos: v. (past of strow, an older form of strew; scattered; spread abroad)
etymology: Saxon streowian, to scatter or spread. Strow is the older spelling of strew; the Authorized Version keeps both.
biblical_def: Josiah is purging Judah, and the purge is thorough: “And they brake down the altars of Baalim in his presence; and the images, that were on high above them, he cut down; and the groves, and the carved images, and the molten images, he brake in pieces, and made dust of them, and strowed it upon the graves of them that had sacrificed unto them” (2 Chronicles 34:4). The idols are not stored, sold, or displayed. They are broken, ground to powder, and the powder scattered over the graves of the men who had worshipped them. The gesture is deliberate and it is a sermon: the god and his worshipper lie in the same dust. Moses had done the same with the golden calf, grinding it and making Israel drink it (Exodus 32:20). Josiah was in the twelfth year of his reign and still a young man (2 Chronicles 34:3), which is the Chronicler's point — reformation began early and went to the root. The dictionary follows the Chronicler's verdict: Josiah was a faithful king, and the mark of his faithfulness is that he did not negotiate with the high places. Half-measures leave idols standing; strowed is what finished obedience looks like.

corruption_paragraphs: The live misuse is curatorial. Idols broken by the reformers are now exhibited as heritage, and the reformers themselves are faulted for vandalism. Scripture is not neutral about the carved image: Josiah ground it to dust, and the Chronicler calls him faithful for it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is thoroughness in repentance. Josiah did not leave the groves for a later reign; he made dust of the images and scattered the dust on the graves. An idol kept in a cupboard is an idol kept.

pos: v. (past of fell; cut down; brought to the ground)
etymology: Saxon fellan, the causative of fall — to make a thing fall. In 2 Kings 3:25 it renders the Hebrew naphal in its causative form, to cause to fall.
biblical_def: The allied kings of Israel, Judah, and Edom carry the war into Moab, and the campaign is described in four strokes: “And they beat down the cities, and on every good piece of land cast every man his stone, and filled it; and they stopped all the wells of water, and felled all the good trees” (2 Kings 3:25). Fields ruined with stones, wells stopped, good trees cut down. The reader is meant to feel the weight of it, because Deuteronomy had put a fence around exactly this: “thou shalt not destroy the trees thereof by forcing an axe against them” (Deuteronomy 20:19). The law allowed siege but forbade the felling of fruit trees — war was not to be waged against the land itself or against generations unborn. The Authorized Version uses felled once, and it sits in a chapter where Israel wins the battle and the narrative closes in a sour note of great indignation. Elisha had promised the victory; the manner of it was Israel's own. Scripture records what men did without commending it, and the restraint the law commanded is the standard by which the campaign is read.

corruption_paragraphs: The verse is sometimes read as divine approval of total war, since Elisha had promised the victory. That confuses promise with permission. Scripture reports what the allied kings did; Deuteronomy 20:19 had already forbidden the felling of fruit trees in a siege, and the law is not suspended because the battle was granted.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is restraint in lawful conflict. A war a man is right to fight he may still fight wrongly, and God's law fences even the victor's axe.

pos: v. (past of overrun; ran past; outran)
etymology: English over and run. In 2 Samuel 18:23 it has its plain older sense: to run past another on the road.
biblical_def: Ahimaaz will not be kept from carrying the news of Absalom's death, though Joab warns him there is no reward in it. “But howsoever, said he, let me run. And he said unto him, Run. Then Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran Cushi” (2 Samuel 18:23). Cushi had been sent first; Ahimaaz took the level road and passed him. The Authorized Version uses overran here alone, and in its older sense — not to invade or flood, but simply to outrun. What makes the verse worth an entry is what the runner carried. Ahimaaz arrives first and cannot say the thing he ran to say; he reports a tumult and stands aside, and Cushi comes behind him with the word that breaks the king: “O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee” (2 Samuel 18:33). Eagerness to be first is not the same as fitness to speak. The young man who overran the Cushite had nothing to deliver when he arrived. Scripture quietly reproves the appetite for being the bearer of news, and sets against it David's grief, which is the one honest thing in the chapter.

corruption_paragraphs: The one misreading worth naming is admiration. Ahimaaz is sometimes held up as a model of zeal. He was zealous and he was useless: he arrived first and had nothing to say. Zeal without a message, and without the standing to carry it, is simply speed.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a messenger is made by his message, not by his legs. Proverbs 29:20 sets a hasty tongue below a fool's, and David's lament over Absalom is the only voice in the chapter that tells the truth.
roots_summary: From over and run, in the older sense of running past another; used of Ahimaaz outrunning Cushi.
